title: Chaitanya and the Bengal kirtan
hook: humbler than a blade of grass, more patient than a tree

segments.voice: Yesterday, kirtan: a scholar set down his arguments and took God's names into the street. What did you join? Day nine hundred thirty-four.

Step on a blade of grass and it bends flat. Lift your foot and, after a moment, it stands back up. No complaint, no grudge. A tree does something similar in the heat: it stands in the sun all day and gives its shade to whoever sits down, including the one with the axe. Those two humble things, grass and a tree, open a short verse that Chaitanya's tradition treasures. Today, on the last day of the saints of bhakti, it answers a practical question: how do you keep singing?
screen: `GRASS BENDS, THEN STANDS.` → `A TREE GIVES ITS SHADE.` → `HOW DO YOU KEEP SINGING?`

segments.voice: Chaitanya's followers keep a short set of verses under his name, called the Shikshashtakam, his teaching. One of them goes, in plain English: be humbler than a blade of grass, more patient than a tree. Give honor to others, and ask none for yourself. Then you can sing the name of Hari always. Read it as the fine print under yesterday's kirtan. Anyone can join the song on the first try. Staying in it is harder. Pride wants the lead line. Impatience wants the song to end. Wanting respect turns a chorus into a competition. The verse clears all three away, and what's left can keep singing. His tradition remembers him living it out in Puri, on the coast, where he spent his later years near the temple of Jagannath. At the great chariot festival, the Ratha Yatra, he is remembered dancing in front of the rolling chariot with groups of kirtan singers, lost in the names, the whole crowd caught up with him. Now look back at the road we've walked these four weeks. Andal and Nammalvar, singing to Vishnu in Tamil. The Nayanars, singing to Shiva. Jnaneshwar, Namdev and Tukaram, walking and singing in Maharashtra. Kabir and his sharp couplets. Tulsidas and Hanuman's song. Surdas in Yashoda's yard. Mira, laughing over the cup. And Chaitanya in the street with a drum. Different languages, different names for God. One habit: they sang to God as if God were near. Next, the modern teachers, beginning with a temple priest near Calcutta and a schoolteacher with a notebook.
screen: `HUMBLER THAN GRASS.` · `MORE PATIENT THAN A TREE.` · `DANCING BEFORE THE CHARIOT.` · then, large: `THEY SANG AS IF GOD WERE NEAR.`

segments.voice: Sit, and feel where your body meets the floor or the chair. For a minute, be like grass: low, rooted, flexible. Breathe in, and as you breathe out, let go of one small need to be right, or to be noticed, today. Breathe in again. Now be like the tree, standing in the sun so others can rest in your shade. Bring to mind one person you could honor today without needing anything back. Hold them in your attention. If you pray, you can let a name of God ride gently on the breath. The bell holds the time.
Shikshashtakam. Chaitanya's short teaching verses, the fine print that keeps the song going: humbler than grass, more patient than a tree.
Your line: humbler than grass. Today, give honor to one person and ask none back, and notice whether the song goes easier. Day nine hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: Gaudiya Vaishnavas recite the Shikshashtakam, and the grass-and-tree verse is often sung or quoted before kirtan; at Puri's Ratha Yatra, kirtan groups sing and dance before Jagannath's chariot.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: a blade of grass, the image that opens the verse on humility.

trapdoor: what you thought: be humble, like a doormat.
what it means: humility, patience and honoring others are what let a person keep singing God's name.
what a scholar hears: the verse belongs to the Shikshashtakam, which the Chaitanya Charitamrita preserves, and it names the conditions for chanting always.
recall: watching until the dust is gone
